findings.title: Cleanup ticker interval reduced from 10 minutes to 1 minute, affecting all cleanup jobs
findings.body: The ticker interval was changed from `time.Minute * 10` to `time.Minute * 1`. This increases the execution frequency of ALL cleanup jobs (snapshots, dashboard versions, images, user invites, short URLs, query history) by 10x, not just annotation cleanup. The PR description only discusses fixing annotation deadlocks and does not mention intentionally changing the global cleanup cadence. This appears to be a debugging or testing change left in accidentally. Running all cleanup jobs every minute will significantly increase database load and may ironically cause more lock contention.

findings.title: Error-level logging used for normal operational messages
findings.body: Lines 534, 537, 554, 557, 576, and 579 all use `r.log.Error(...)` to log routine operational information (e.g., 'Annotations to clean by time', 'cleaned annotations by time', 'Tags to clean'). At this point in the code, `err` is nil (errors were already checked and returned above). Using Error level for non-error conditions will pollute error monitoring and alerting systems in production, making it harder to identify real issues. These should be `r.log.Debug` or `r.log.Info`.

findings.title: Logging all annotation IDs can produce extremely large log entries
findings.body: The log statements include `"ids", ids` which serializes the entire slice of fetched IDs. With `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` configured up to 32767 (as tested), this produces log lines containing tens of thousands of integers on every batch iteration. This will cause significant log volume and potential performance issues in production. Consider logging only the count or a truncated sample of IDs.

findings.title: Loop may terminate prematurely when IDs are fetched but already deleted by concurrent processes
findings.body: In `untilDoneOrCancelled`, the loop exits when `affected == 0`. With the new split approach, it's possible that `fetchIDs` returns a non-empty list of IDs, but by the time `deleteByIDs` executes, those rows have already been deleted by another process (e.g., a concurrent cleanup instance or explicit user deletion). In this case `affected` is 0 and the loop stops, even though more eligible rows may exist. While the next cleanup cycle will handle them, with the original 10-minute interval this could mean a 10-minute delay in cleanup. The 1-minute ticker change may have been an attempt to mitigate this, but the root cause is that the termination condition should be based on whether `fetchIDs` returned results, not whether the delete affected rows.
